title: Using High Resolution Secondary Electron Imaging to Build a Complete Picture of High Temperature Processes
content: In situ microscopy has enabled an extreme amount of progress in understanding transformations of materials under various conditions [1]. In particular, imaging thermal processes have garnered a substantial amount of research interest in order to observe the degradation of materials as well as material formation at elevated temperatures [2, 3]. A vast majority of these experiments revolve around using high kV (200–300kV) scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM), which have generated a vast amount of data showing the heat-induced changes to the atomic structure and morphology of materials. As incredible as these results are, they leave extremely crucial gaps within our understanding of various materials under high heat. These gaps include a lack of high-resolution images that show surface details and the observation of transformations happening in very thick deposition regions, i.e. to dense for the beam to penetrate. It is in these cases that imaging in the low kV regime whilst collecting primarily secondary electron images at high resolution can bridge this knowledge gap. In Figure 1 a schematic of these two specific types of areas can be seen on a rendering of an in situ heating chip, featuring thick deposition regions highlighted on the left (green) and surface changes that occur to materials on the right (red).
